title: RBI Governor Says Rupee Is Undervalued as FCNR(B) Inflows Cross $32 Billion
excerpt: Sanjay Malhotra dismisses deposit recycling concerns and says the central bank has 'foolproof' hedging against currency risk from the inflow drive.
body:
• Banks have mobilised nearly $32 billion through FCNR(B) deposits since the RBI's June measures, with government securities attracting over $7 billion in foreign inflows
  • RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the rupee does not reflect weakness in India's economic fundamentals and is under pressure primarily from geopolitics and dollar strength
  • Malhotra dismissed concerns about the RBI bearing hedging costs, saying the central bank has a 'foolproof system' of insuring itself through foreign asset investments
  • Some banks are offering FCNR(B) rates as high as 7.5%, well above domestic deposit rates, with the RBI absorbing the hedging cost through September

Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra has said the rupee is undervalued relative to India's economic fundamentals, as the central bank's aggressive push to attract foreign currency deposits continues to yield results — with banks mobilising nearly $32 billion, largely through FCNR(B) deposits, since June.

What the Inflow Numbers Show

The RBI's package of measures, announced alongside the June monetary policy meeting, has drawn a strong investor response. Banks have raised the bulk of the $32 billion through Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits, while government securities have attracted more than $7 billion in foreign portfolio inflows, according to Malhotra.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rJwU8nMvE6I

The State Bank of India's research department initially estimated the measures could attract $55–65 billion in total. The current pace suggests the programme is on track, though analysts at Reuters noted the RBI may have used part of the initial inflows to unwind a portion of its record $106.6 billion short-dollar forward book rather than directly boosting reserves.

IDFC First Bank chief economist Gaura Sen Gupta estimated India's balance of payments is tracking a surplus of around $25 billion, though she cautioned this assumed Brent crude averaging $75–80 per barrel — well below current prices near $100.

What NRI Depositors Are Getting

The RBI removed interest rate ceilings on FCNR(B) deposits in June, allowing banks to offer rates as high as 7.5 percent on three-to-five-year dollar deposits — significantly above both domestic Indian deposit rates and US Treasury yields of around 4.2 percent for comparable tenors.

"It is not something which should be a matter of concern because we have a foolproof system of insuring ourselves. Whatever dollars we get, the excess foreign currency is invested in foreign assets."

— RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra, on hedging risks from FCNR(B) inflows

The central bank is bearing the full hedging cost of the deposits through September 30, effectively guaranteeing banks against currency depreciation risk. Critics, including a Hindu BusinessLine analysis, have warned that the leverage permitted on these deposits — with some banks offering nine to 19 times leverage — could create future risks if the rupee depreciates sharply when the deposits mature.

Rupee Outlook

Malhotra pushed back against market concerns about rupee weakness, arguing that recent depreciation stemmed from geopolitical tensions — particularly the US-Iran conflict — dollar strength, and broader emerging market volatility rather than any deterioration in India's economic position.

The rupee has traded near record lows against the dollar in recent weeks, pressured by oil prices climbing toward $100 per barrel. Societe Generale strategists noted that the oil surge has offset the positive impact of the RBI's inflow measures, keeping the currency on the defensive despite heavy central bank intervention in both onshore and offshore markets.

For NRIs considering FCNR(B) deposits, the window remains attractive: the combination of high interest rates, RBI-backed hedging, and potential leverage makes it one of the most lucrative fixed-income opportunities available. But the underlying message from Malhotra is clear — the central bank views the current exchange rate as temporary and expects the rupee to recover as global conditions stabilise.
